headline: Rates Fall to Two-Week Low as Stocks Tumble
tileReason: The daily 30-year average fell to 7.33% Friday, its lowest since Nov 10, as a steep stock selloff sent investors into bonds; yields are edging back up this morning as stocks rebound.
takeaway:
Rates had their best day in weeks on Friday. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average fell to 7.33% from 7.45% Thursday, a drop of 0.12% and the lowest level since Nov 10, and several lenders cut rates in the middle of the day. Other surveys taken Friday point the same way: Zillow showed 7.18% and the Mortgage Research Center about 7.20%.

A stock market rout did the work. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% Friday and about 8.6% for the week, as worries about artificial intelligence spending hammered big tech stocks. Investors fleeing stocks bought Treasury bonds for safety, and the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, closed Friday near 4.92%, down from 5.04% Thursday and about 0.23% lower for the week.

This time lenders passed more of it along. Last week bonds improved after most lenders had already set their rates, so the daily average moved only a hair. Friday's bond rally came early and kept going, which gave lenders room to lower rates during the day.

Some of that is reversing this morning. Stock futures are up about 2.5% after the selloff paused overnight, and the 10-year yield has climbed back to roughly 4.96%, up about 0.04% (sources range from 4.93% to 4.96%). If that holds, today's rates could give back a little of Friday's drop. New York Fed President John Williams speaks at 1 PM PT, and Treasury Secretary Bessent warned over the weekend against raising rates too far while markets are shaky.

A December Fed hike is still the expectation, but the bigger-hike talk has faded. Futures markets, where traders bet on the Fed's next move, put the odds of a quarter-point increase in the Fed's short-term rate on Dec 9 somewhere between about 91% and 96% over the weekend and this morning, depending on the source. The rest is now on no change at all, rather than on the bigger half-point hike Governor Waller floated last week. These are market expectations, not a Fed forecast.

Lenders still have a cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 17, the latest day recorded, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room means lenders don't have to pass along every bit of a bond selloff, and it leaves room for further improvement if bonds hold their gains.

This is a short week with a big test. Wednesday morning brings the Fed's preferred inflation measure (PCE, a broad gauge of consumer prices), expected to show prices up 3.8% from a year earlier, plus a second look at third-quarter growth. Bond markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early Friday. After that: the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

drivers.title: Stock rout sends money into bonds
drivers.text: The S&P 500 fell 3.7% Friday and about 8.6% for the week on worries about AI spending. Investors moving money from stocks into Treasury bonds pushed bond prices up and yields down, and the 10-year yield closed near 4.92%, its lowest in weeks, helping mortgage rates drop 0.12%.

drivers.title: Stocks bounce back this morning
drivers.text: Stock futures are up about 2.5% this morning as the selloff paused, and some of the money that ran to bonds is heading back out. That pushed the 10-year yield back up to about 4.96%, which could take back part of Friday's rate drop.

drivers.title: Fed still expected to hike in December
drivers.text: Markets still see a quarter-point Fed hike on Dec 9 as very likely, and Fed minutes showed almost all officials expect more increases. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling far. The odds of a bigger half-point hike have faded, which helps a little.

drivers.title: Inflation still running hot
drivers.text: October consumer prices beat forecasts for the third month in a row, and Wednesday's report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure is expected to show prices up 3.8% from a year earlier. Bond investors demand higher yields when inflation eats into what their interest is worth, and mortgage rates follow.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 17, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields, and have room to lower rates if bonds hold their gains.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 20 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even, tilted slightly higher because rates start from Friday's two-week low and yields are rising this morning. Mortgage rates fell to 7.33% as a stock rout drove investors into bonds, but stocks are bouncing back today. In borrowers' favor: shaky stocks, fading talk of a bigger Fed hike, and mortgage rates still sit unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.19% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Working against borrowers: a December Fed hike is still widely expected and inflation reports keep running hot, so a steady stock recovery or a hot report could undo Friday's gains quickly. Big swing events: the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision, Dec 10 consumer prices and oil headlines.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: Mortgage rates had their best day in weeks Friday, with the daily 30-year average dropping to 7.33%, the lowest since Nov 10. Yields are climbing back a bit this morning as stocks rebound, and a December Fed hike is still expected, so the next few weeks could be bumpy. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates just dipped to a two-week low around 7.33%, a small break for buyers heading into the holidays. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out while buyers are watching every payment.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates fell to a two-week low near 7.33% Friday as a stock selloff pushed bond yields down, though yields are edging back up this morning.
